newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Nobel prize puts spotlight on troubled East Timor.
newsitem.headline: Nobel prize puts spotlight on troubled East Timor.

text.p: The award of the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize to two men born in East Timor whose lives have been overshadowed by its struggle for independence is a reminder of the troubled history of the former Portuguese colony.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced on Friday the joint award of the peace prize to the territory's Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and exiled independence movement leader Jose Ramos-Horta.
Indonesia invaded mainly Catholic East Timor on December 7, 1975, after civil war erupted on the equatorial island following the withdrawal of Portuguese authorities four months earlier.
Indonesian airborne and ground troops toppled the leftist Fretilin party, which had established a de facto government and issued an independence proclamation.

Ramos-Horta at the time was Fretilin's secretary for foreign affairs and information, but fled three days before the Indonesian invasion. He now lives in Australia and ensures the resistance to Indonesian rule is given an international profile.
Belo, who was appointed bishop in 1983 reporting directly to the Pope in the Vatican, walks a thin line between his flock and the Jakarta-appointed administration.
Human rights groups said up to one third of the population, or about 200,000 people, died during the invasion and subsequent fighting and famine in East Timor.
The invasion took place just after a visit by then U.S President Gerald Ford to Jakarta, capital of mainly Moslem Indonesia and some 2,000 km (1,200 miles) west of East Timor.
Indonesia's President Suharto said later he could not tolerate "a Cuba in our backyard".
The Portuguese set up a trading outpost on the eastern half of Timor island, straddling a shipping route between Australia and the huge island of New Guinea, early in the 16th century.
They found the island a plentiful source of sandalwood, prized for its aroma and medicinal oil.
A division of the island in the 19th century gave Portugal the east, while the Netherlands, the colonial power in the rest of the old East Indies islands, was given the remainder.
Japanese and Australian troops fought fierce battles on the Portuguese half of Timor during World War Two, in which up to 60,000 East Timorese were killed.
The Allies feared Japan would use the island as a base to launch an invasion of Australia.
After the war, Portugal rehabilitated the coffee and sandalwood plantations but left the island largely undeveloped.
After a military coup ended some four decades of right-wing dictatorship in Portugal in April 1974, the new leftist government sought to discard remnants of the country's colonial empire.
It hastily withdrew from East Timor, roughly the size of Northern Ireland, sparking civil war.
Indonesia declared East Timor its 27th province on July 17, 1976, seven months after the invasion, having pushed Fretilin insurgents into the hills.
The United Nations has never recognised the takeover and still regards Portugal as the administering power.
Fretilin guerrillas mounted regular attacks on Indonesian troops for years after the invasion from their hideouts in the rugged, mountainous interior.
Up to 80 percent of the Timorese abandoned, or were forced to leave, their homes during the fighting, witnesses and human rights activists said.
Today, the government and foreign military sources put the number of Fretilin guerrillas at less than 200.
On November 12, 1991, witnesses said Indonesian troops in Dili, East Timor's capital, killed up to 200 protesters marching to the grave of a Timorese activist killed by troops.
An Indonesian commission of inquiry on December 26, 1991, revised the official toll from 19 to "about 50" and said the protesters acted belligerently and showed liberation banners.
In November 1994, on the third anniversary of the Dili massacre, 29 Timorese students climbed the railings of the U.S. embassy in Jakarta for a sit-in to demand Gusmao's release.
The students later won asylum in Portugal, as did about 90 young Timorese who have staged a series of break-ins in several foreign embassies in Jakarta since September 1995.
In January 1995, East Timor was under the human rights spotlight again after the killings of six East Timorese by soldiers near Liquisa. Two soldiers were later jailed.
The territory has been free of large scale violence in 1996, although youths have held protests after the shooting of two men in March by security authorities near Baucau and Dili.
A further alleged shooting last month has also raised tension and prompted an outcry among Timorese youth, particularly those living on Java.
